introduction-the-dark-data-problem.core: Organisations accumulate thousands of tables nobody can find, understand or trust: 'dark data'. Without metadata on what exists, who owns it and where it came from, teams duplicate work, use wrong data and can't assess change impact or compliance.

first_principles.problem: Three teams build three slightly different 'active users' tables, and nobody knows which is correct.
truths: Regulations require knowing where personal data lives.

analogy.title: A library with books piled on the floor
analogy.story: Everything's technically there, but without an index you can't find or trust anything.
analogy.breaks: Books don't change; datasets are rewritten daily, so metadata must update automatically.

example.title: The three 'active users' tables
example.outcome: data people can find and trust.

check.a: Data that exists but can't be found, understood or trusted because it lacks metadata.

the-data-catalog-google-for-your-data.core: A data catalog (DataHub, Amundsen, OpenMetadata, Unity Catalog) is a searchable portal of datasets with schemas, descriptions, owners, tags, popularity, quality status and glossary terms, so people can discover data and judge whether to trust it.

first_principles.problem: Analysts spend days asking on Slack which table to use.
truths: Trust signals include ownership, freshness and usage.
Business terms differ from table names.

analogy.title: Google search for company data
analogy.story: Type 'revenue', get ranked results with descriptions and who to ask.
analogy.breaks: Google crawls public pages; a catalog must be fed from internal systems and kept curated.

example.title: Finding the right revenue table
flow: Top hit: certified, owned by finance, fresh 2 h ago

check.q: Name three trust signals a catalog shows.
check.a: Owner, freshness/quality status and certification or usage popularity.

data-lineage-the-family-tree-of-your-dat.core: Lineage is the directed graph of how data flows: source → transformations → tables → dashboards and models. Upstream lineage answers 'where did this come from?' (debugging); downstream answers 'what breaks if I change this?' (impact analysis), ideally down to column level.

first_principles.problem: An engineer renames a column and silently breaks twelve dashboards and a model.
truths: Data products depend on each other.
derivation: Capture edges from **SQL parsing, orchestrators and runtime events** (OpenLineage).

analogy.title: A family tree
analogy.story: It tells you both your ancestors and your descendants.
analogy.breaks: Family trees are fixed; lineage changes with every pipeline deploy.

example.title: Impact analysis before a rename
flow: Downstream query: 3 dbt models, 12 dashboards, 1 feature
example.outcome: safe change with known blast radius.

check.q: What question does downstream lineage answer?
check.a: What reports, models and tables will be affected if this dataset or column changes.

architecture-pull-vs-push-metadata.core: Catalogs get metadata by pull (crawlers periodically scan databases and warehouses) or push (systems emit metadata events as they run, e.g. OpenLineage from Airflow or Spark). Pull is easy to start but stale and coarse; push is fresh and precise but needs instrumentation. Most platforms combine both.

first_principles.problem: A nightly crawler leaves the catalog up to 24 hours stale and misses runtime lineage.
truths: Runtime systems know what they read and wrote.
derivation: **Pull**: scheduled crawlers for schemas and stats.
**Combine**: crawl for coverage, push for freshness and lineage.

analogy.title: A census versus a birth registry
analogy.story: The census counts everyone every ten years; the registry records each birth when it happens.
analogy.breaks: A census reaches everyone; push only covers instrumented systems.

example.title: Hybrid ingestion
flow: Airflow emits OpenLineage on each run
Catalog shows schema plus live lineage

check.q: What's the main weakness of pull-based metadata?
check.a: It's only as fresh as the last crawl and can miss runtime lineage.
